config.method: learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors combined with frozen strong-model margin priors, refined via two EM rounds

finding: On the chat_preference testbed, we evaluated a weak-to-strong training pipeline that pairs a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors with frozen strong-model margin priors, refined through two rounds of EM. The single reported metric is a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.78. This figure should be read with substantial caution. No baseline PGR was supplied, so we cannot characterize the result as an improvement over any comparison method, nor can we say how much of the 0.78 is attributable to the noisy-channel component, the margin priors, or the EM refinement, since no ablations were run. The configuration also omits num_seeds, meaning the number of independent runs behind the 0.78 is unknown, and no standard error or variance estimate accompanies it; the value may therefore reflect a single run and could shift under reseeding. Additional runs with seed counts recorded, a stated baseline, and component ablations are needed before drawing inferences about the method's effectiveness.

config.method: measures per-sample loss drop over training as a learnability signal, applies adaptive label smoothing weighted by that signal

finding: We evaluated a method that measures per-sample loss drop over training as a learnability signal and applies adaptive label smoothing weighted by that signal, on the chat_preference testbed. The single reported metric is a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.62. Several important caveats limit what can be concluded from this. No baseline PGR was provided, so we cannot say whether this value represents an improvement over an existing or naive approach — the 0.62 figure stands alone and is uninterpretable as a gain. The configuration also reports no seed count (num_seeds is absent), so we have no information about run-to-run variance, and no standard error or confidence interval accompanies the point estimate. Results are furthermore confined to a single testbed, so generalization to other preference or classification settings is untested. The finding should therefore be read as a preliminary, single-number observation that motivates a properly seeded comparison against a stated baseline rather than as evidence that the learnability-weighted smoothing approach works.

config.method: two-phase curriculum: train on most-confident half first, then continue on full data at lower learning rate

finding: On the chat_preference testbed, a two-phase curriculum — training first on the most-confident half of the data, then continuing on the full dataset at a lower learning rate — yielded a PGR of 0.68. This is the only metric reported for the run, and it should be read with substantial caution. The configuration does not specify num_seeds, so the number of replicates behind this value is unknown and no estimate of run-to-run variability is available; a single reported figure cannot be distinguished from noise without such information. No baseline PGR is provided either, so the 0.68 cannot be characterized as better or worse than a standard one-phase training procedure, nor can any gain be attributed to the curriculum structure or the reduced learning rate in the second phase. Further runs with multiple seeds and a matched baseline would be needed before drawing any comparative conclusion about this method's effect.

config.method: selects training examples by alignment between weak labels and strong-model embedding geometry, then fine-tunes on the top-scoring half

finding: On the chat_preference testbed, we evaluated a method that scores training examples by the alignment between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry, retains the top-scoring half, and fine-tunes on that subset. The run yielded a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.75. Several caveats materially limit what can be drawn from this. The configuration reports no num_seeds, so the number of replicates behind the 0.75 figure is unknown and no variance or standard error is available; we therefore cannot assess run-to-run spread or attach any uncertainty interval to the point estimate. No baseline PGR is provided either, so the 0.75 cannot be characterized as an improvement over an unfiltered or randomly filtered fine-tuning control, nor over any other selection strategy. The result is best read as a single reported measurement on one testbed, pending repeated seeds and a matched baseline before any comparative or confidence claim is made.

config.method: an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student

finding: We evaluated an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student (aux_loss_weight 0.1) in a weak-to-strong setup where gpt2-small supervises mistral-7b, across num_seeds = 8 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.62 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy is 0.81, while the strong student trained on weak labels attains a transfer accuracy of 0.63 (SE 0.02). The resulting performance gap recovered is 0.03 with a standard error of 0.13, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.12. The measured PGR therefore sits below the baseline, and in any case the standard error on PGR is far larger than the quantity itself, so these data do not support any claim that the auxiliary confidence loss helps; the result is compatible with no effect in either direction. The transfer accuracy estimate is much more tightly determined than the PGR, suggesting that the PGR noise stems largely from the narrow weak-to-strong accuracy range. Further seeds would be needed to resolve the direction of the effect.

config.method: confidence regularization on the student's predictions

finding: We evaluated confidence regularization on the student's predictions (confidence_reg_weight = 1.0) in a weak-to-strong setting where gpt2-small supervises qwen2.5-3b, across 5 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.5 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy is 0.84, while the regularized student transfers to 0.55 accuracy (SE 0.02). This corresponds to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.15 with a standard error of 0.05, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.32. The measured PGR therefore falls below the baseline rather than above it, so this experiment provides no evidence that confidence regularization helps here; if anything it points the other way, though we report the comparison as observed and do not treat the shortfall as established, since only a single baseline value is given without its own uncertainty estimate. With 5 seeds and a PGR standard error of 0.05, precision remains limited, and the result should be read as a preliminary signal at this single regularization weight.

config.method: label smoothing on the weak supervision targets

finding: We evaluated label smoothing on the weak supervision targets (label_smoothing = 0.05) in a weak-to-strong setup pairing a pythia-410m weak supervisor with a qwen2.5-7b strong student, averaged over 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.47 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.65, while the strong student trained on smoothed weak labels achieved transfer accuracy of 0.57 with a standard error of 0.01. This corresponds to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.54 with a standard error of 0.02, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.47. The gain over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the direction of the effect is supported by these 10 seeds, though the margin is modest and only the point estimate for the baseline is available, with no reported uncertainty for it. Results are limited to this single model pair, smoothing value, and task setup, so generalization to other configurations remains untested.

config.method: early stopping on weak-label validation loss

finding: We evaluated early stopping on weak-label validation loss on the sciq testbed across num_seeds = 3 seeds, obtaining a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.02. This value indicates that the method recovered almost none of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling on this testbed, so the procedure as configured does not appear to extract much additional capability from the strong student beyond its weak labels. Two caveats should temper any reading of this number. First, with only three seeds and no reported standard error or variance, the precision of the 0.02 estimate is unknown, and we cannot characterize how much it would move under reseeding. Second, no baseline PGR was supplied for comparison, so we make no claim that this configuration improves on or underperforms any alternative. A larger seed count, reported dispersion, and a matched baseline would be needed before drawing firm conclusions about early stopping on weak-label validation loss.

config.method: bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model

finding: We evaluated bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model, using gpt2-small as the weak supervisor, qwen2.5-1.5b as the intermediate model, and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student, across num_seeds = 3 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.6 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling (trained on ground truth) is 0.82, while the bootstrapped transfer accuracy is 0.63 with a standard error of 0.03. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) is 0.14 with a standard error of 0.14, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.24 for direct weak-to-strong training. The measured PGR is therefore below the baseline and its standard error is as large as the point estimate itself, so these data provide no evidence that the intermediate-model bootstrapping pipeline recovers more of the gap than the baseline; with only three seeds the estimate is too imprecise to rank the two methods in either direction. Further seeds would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion.

config.method: training only on the most confidently weak-labeled examples

finding: We tested whether restricting strong-model training to the most confidently weak-labeled examples improves weak-to-strong generalization, using gpt2-small as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student with a keep_fraction of 0.7. Across 3 seeds, the weak supervisor reached 0.64 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.91, while the confidence-filtered transfer run reached 0.63 accuracy (SE 0.02) and a PGR of -0.05 (SE 0.09). This sits below the baseline PGR of 0.16, so the filtering approach shows no advantage here; indeed the negative central estimate suggests the student recovered none of the gap between weak and strong performance, though with an SE of 0.09 the PGR interval is wide enough that little can be resolved either way. With only 3 seeds, these numbers should be read as preliminary and not as evidence about the method's general behavior. Replication with more seeds and additional keep_fraction settings would be needed before drawing conclusions.

config.method: selecting training examples by agreement between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry

finding: We tested a weak-to-strong generalization setup in which gpt2-small supplies weak labels for llama-3.1-8b, and training examples are filtered by agreement between the weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry, retaining a select_fraction of 0.5. Across num_seeds = 10 seeds, the method reached a PGR of 0.69 with a standard error of 0.09, against a baseline PGR of 0.49; the baseline falls outside two standard errors of the selection-based estimate, so the data support treating this as a genuine gain rather than seed noise, though the standard error is large enough that the magnitude should be read loosely. Transfer accuracy was 0.73 (SE 0.02), situated between the weak ceiling of 0.61 and the strong model's 0.78, indicating the strong student surpasses its weak supervisor without matching strong-label training. No baseline transfer accuracy or standard error for the baseline PGR was reported, which limits direct comparison on the accuracy scale.

config.method: a two-phase curriculum from confident to full weak-labeled data

finding: Using a two-phase curriculum that begins with confident weak-labeled examples and then expands to the full weak-labeled set, with the second phase run at a learning-rate scale of 0.1, we measure a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.82 on the ANLI testbed. This figure is averaged over num_seeds = 4 seeds, which is a small sample, and no per-seed spread or standard error was recorded, so the run-to-run variability of this number is unknown from the data at hand. Importantly, no baseline PGR was supplied for comparison, so this result cannot be characterized as an improvement over single-phase training on the full weak-labeled data or over any other reference method; it stands only as a standalone measurement of the curriculum configuration described. Establishing whether the two-phase schedule and the reduced phase-two learning rate contribute anything would require a matched baseline, additional seeds, and reported variance.

config.method: adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop

finding: Using gpt2-small as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student, we evaluated adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop, with smoothing_max set to 0.3, across num_seeds = 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.56 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.74, while the strongly-supervised-equivalent transfer accuracy under weak labels was 0.73 with a standard error of 0.01. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.93 with a standard error of 0.05, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.23. The margin between the method's PGR and the baseline is substantially larger than two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the recovery under this method exceeds the baseline by more than sampling noise would explain. Caveats: the baseline PGR is reported without an accompanying standard error, so the comparison rests on the method's uncertainty alone, and results come from a single weak–strong model pair and one smoothing_max setting, leaving generality untested.

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

finding: We evaluated a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states, read out at probe layer 24, with qwen2.5-3b as the strong model and qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor, across num_seeds = 4 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.56 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.84, while the probe-based transfer attains 0.79 accuracy with a standard error of 0.05. The resulting performance gap recovered is 0.82 with a standard error of 0.19, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.18. Although the measured PGR is numerically far above the baseline, the uncertainty is substantial relative to that margin and only four seeds were run, so this should be read as a suggestive rather than an established effect. The large standard error on PGR also indicates seed-to-seed variability that a larger run would be needed to characterize. No results for other layers, model pairs, or task distributions are reported here, so generality remains untested.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: In this weak-to-strong generalization setup, a qwen2.5-3b student was fine-tuned on labels from a gpt2-small supervisor, with the student's fine-tune restricted to a low-rank adapter of rank 4. The weak supervisor reached 0.46 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.62, while the student trained on weak labels achieved a transfer accuracy of 0.54 with a standard error of 0.01. The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.53 with a standard error of 0.03, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.33. An important caveat is that these numbers come from num_seeds = 1, so the reported standard errors rest on a single run and give no information about seed-to-seed variability; the apparent separation from the baseline should therefore be treated as provisional rather than established. Replication across additional seeds, and ideally across other weak-strong model pairs and adapter ranks, would be needed before attributing the difference to the low-rank restriction itself.

config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: On HellaSwag, we evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels across 16 seeds, obtaining a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.04. This indicates that the procedure recovers roughly half of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling, with the seed-to-seed spread being fairly tight at this sample size. An important caveat is that no baseline PGR was supplied in the data provided, so we cannot characterize this value as an improvement over, or a regression from, standard weak-to-strong training or any alternative method; the 0.49 figure should be read as a standalone measurement rather than as evidence that repeated self-distillation helps. The result is also specific to a single testbed, and no per-seed values, task-level breakdowns, or ceiling and supervisor accuracies were available for inspection. Comparative runs under matched conditions would be needed before drawing any conclusion about the method's relative merit.

config.method: reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin

finding: We tested weak-to-strong generalization by reweighting weak labels according to the frozen strong model's margin, with a margin temperature of 0.5, training qwen2.5-7b on labels from gpt2-small. The weak supervisor reaches 0.6 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.82; the strong model trained on reweighted weak labels reaches a transfer accuracy of 0.78 (SE 0.03), corresponding to a PGR of 0.81 with a standard error of 0.14, against a baseline PGR of 0.26. Importantly, this comes from a single seed (num_seeds = 1), so the reported standard errors rest on one run and give no information about seed-to-seed variability; no baseline standard error is provided, so the comparison with 0.26 cannot be assessed against two standard errors of the baseline. The direction is encouraging, but the evidence here is preliminary and would need replication across several seeds before the margin-reweighting method could be credited with a genuine gain.

config.method: mixup between weak-labeled examples

finding: We evaluated mixup between weak-labeled examples (mixup_alpha = 0.2) in a weak-to-strong setting with qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across num_seeds = 4 seeds. The weak model reaches 0.55 accuracy and the strong ceiling is 0.77. Training the strong model on weak labels with mixup yields a transfer accuracy of 0.74 (SE 0.04) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.87 with a standard error of 0.16, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.17. The PGR standard error is large relative to the reported value, and with only four seeds the estimate is imprecise; no standard error is provided for the baseline, so the comparison between the two PGR figures cannot be assessed for statistical support here. The direction of the numbers favors mixup, but further seeds and a variance estimate for the baseline would be needed before drawing firm conclusions about the method's effect.

config.method: evolution-strategy refinement using swap-consistency as fitness

finding: We evaluated an evolution-strategy refinement method that uses swap-consistency as its fitness signal, with an ES population size of 16, on the BoolQ testbed. Across 5 seeds, the measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.43. No baseline PGR was supplied with this run, so this number should be read as a standalone measurement rather than as evidence that the method improves on any alternative; without a reference point we cannot characterise the result as a gain. config.method: multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model

config.method: aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning

config.method: randomly dropping a fraction of weak labels each epoch

config.method: a contrastive pretext objective before weak-label fine-tuning

config.method: training only a linear head on frozen strong features

config.method: an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student

config.method: training only on the most confidently weak-labeled examples

config.method: averaging labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors

config.method: a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization

config.method: selecting training examples by agreement between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry

config.method: a two-phase curriculum from confident to full weak-labeled data

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

config.method: early stopping on weak-label validation loss

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

Because the standard error is nearly as large as the point estimate itself, the data are compatible with a PGR at or near zero, and we cannot treat this as evidence that the probe recovers a meaningful share of the gap. No baseline PGR was supplied in this experiment, so there is no reference point against which to assess whether the probe outperforms an alternative weak-to-strong method; any claim of improvement would be unsupported. The 16-seed sample does, however, give a reasonably well-characterized estimate of the spread, and the breadth of that spread is the main finding: the effect, if present, is small relative to seed-to-seed variation. Further seeds or a specified baseline would be needed to draw a directional conclusion.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: We tested whether restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter (LoRA rank 16) changes weak-to-strong generalization, using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 6 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.47 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.67; the LoRA-constrained student trained on weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.56 (SE 0.03), corresponding to a PGR of 0.43 with a standard error of 0.13. The baseline PGR is 0.26, so the observed difference falls within two standard errors of the baseline and cannot be treated as an improvement on this evidence; the direction is favorable but the spread across seeds is wide relative to the gap. With only 6 seeds and a PGR standard error of 0.13, these numbers are best read as suggestive, and a larger seed count would be needed to resolve whether the low-rank restriction helps.

config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: We evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels, run for 2 distill rounds, with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and llama-3.1-8b as the strong student. Across 4 seeds, the method reached a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.82 with a standard error of 0.09, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.05; the margin over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the measured PGR, so the effect is larger than the run-to-run spread we observed. Transfer accuracy was 0.87 (standard error 0.02), sitting between the weak supervisor's accuracy of 0.65 and the strong model's ceiling of 0.92. The main caveat is the small sample: with only 4 seeds, the standard errors are themselves imprecisely estimated, and no baseline standard error is reported, so the comparison rests on the point estimate for the baseline. Results are also specific to this single weak–strong model pairing and to 2 rounds of distillation.

config.method: reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin

finding: We tested weak-to-strong generalization using reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin, with a margin temperature of 1.0, a gpt2-medium weak supervisor, and llama-3.1-8b as the strong student, across 5 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.55 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy was 0.87. Training the strong model on the reweighted weak labels yielded a transfer accuracy of 0.84 (SE 0.04) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.92 with a standard error of 0.11, against a baseline PGR of 0.11. The PGR exceeds the baseline by more than two standard errors, so the margin-based reweighting appears to recover substantially more of the weak-to-strong gap than the baseline under this setup. Caveats: the estimate rests on only 5 seeds and a PGR standard error of 0.11, a single weak/strong model pair, and one margin temperature setting, so the magnitude should be treated as approximate and generalization to other pairings remains untested.

config.method: mixup between weak-labeled examples

finding: We evaluated mixup between weak-labeled examples (mixup_alpha = 0.4) on the cosmos_qa testbed, measuring performance gap recovered (PGR). Across num_seeds = 3 seeds, the method attained a PGR of 0.9 with a standard error of 0.14. Taken at face value, this indicates that the student recovers a large share of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling on this task, but the estimate carries substantial uncertainty: with only three seeds, the standard error of 0.14 is wide relative to the quantity being measured, and the sampling distribution of such a small set of runs is poorly characterized. No baseline PGR was supplied in this experiment, so we cannot characterize the result as an improvement over any alternative weak-to-strong training procedure, nor can we attribute the observed value specifically to the mixup intervention rather than to other aspects of the setup. The finding should be treated as preliminary and worth replicating with more seeds and an explicit baseline arm before any comparative claim is made.

config.method: multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model

finding: We evaluated weak-to-strong generalization using multi-template margin signals drawn from the frozen strong base model, with 8 templates, llama-3.1-8b as the strong model and pythia-410m as the weak supervisor, across 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.65 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.87, while the strong model trained on weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.71 with a standard error of 0.02. This corresponds to a performance gap recovered of 0.26 with a standard error of 0.08, against a baseline PGR of 0.29. The method therefore does not improve on the baseline: the measured PGR falls below it, and the difference is well within two standard errors, so the data are compatible with no difference in either direction. With a PGR standard error of 0.08 over 10 seeds, the resolution here is limited, and these numbers should be read as neutral rather than as evidence for the multi-template margin approach.

config.method: aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning

finding: On the MultiRC testbed, we evaluated aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning with a clip norm of 0.1, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.27 across 8 seeds. This is the full extent of what the data supports: no baseline PGR was recorded for comparison, so the result cannot be characterized as an improvement over, or a regression from, standard fine-tuning without clipping. Nor were per-seed variances or standard errors reported, which means the spread of the eight runs around the 0.27 figure is unknown and no statement about the stability of the effect can be made. The number should therefore be read as a single point estimate from one configuration on one task, with the clip norm of 0.1 untested against alternative values. Establishing whether this clipping intervention helps or hurts would require running an unclipped control under identical conditions and reporting dispersion across seeds alongside the mean.

config.method: randomly dropping a fraction of weak labels each epoch

finding: We tested whether randomly dropping a fraction of weak labels each epoch (label_dropout = 0.3) aids weak-to-strong generalization, supervising a qwen2.5-7b strong model with labels from a pythia-410m weak model. Across num_seeds = 2 seeds, the method yielded a PGR of 0.26 with a standard error of 0.17, against a baseline PGR of 0.53. The strong model's ceiling accuracy was 0.84 and the weak supervisor reached 0.67, while the transfer accuracy under weak supervision was 0.71 with a standard error of 0.03. The measured PGR falls below the baseline, so this run provides no evidence that label dropout helps; with only two seeds and a PGR standard error of 0.17, the estimate is also too imprecise to characterize the apparent shortfall with confidence. We therefore treat this as a preliminary, non-confirmatory observation, and additional seeds would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about label dropout's effect.

config.method: discarding examples where weak supervisors disagree

finding: We evaluated a weak-to-strong generalization method that discards training examples where weak supervisors disagree, using a minimum agreement threshold of 0.8, on the SciQ testbed. Across num_seeds = 2 seeds, the method attained a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.95 with a standard error of 0.03. Taken at face value, this indicates that the strong student recovered most of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling under this filtering scheme. Several caveats limit how far this should be read. No baseline PGR was supplied, so we cannot characterize the result as an improvement over naive weak supervision or any alternative filtering rule; the number stands alone. With only two seeds, the reported standard error rests on a very small sample and the spread across runs is poorly constrained. The finding is also specific to a single testbed and a single agreement threshold, so generalization to other datasets or thresholds remains untested here.

config.method: training only a linear head on frozen strong features

finding: We evaluated weak-to-strong generalization by training only a linear head on frozen strong features, using llama-3.1-8b as the strong model and pythia-410m as the weak supervisor, with a probe learning rate of 0.01 and across num_seeds = 3 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.66 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.83, while the linear probe trained on weak labels achieved a transfer accuracy of 0.69 (SE 0.02). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.18 with a standard error of 0.14, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.28. The measured PGR therefore sits below the baseline, and with only three seeds and a standard error of 0.14 the estimate is too imprecise to support any claim of improvement over the baseline; the difference falls well within two standard errors. These numbers should be read as preliminary, and a larger seed count would be needed to distinguish the linear-probe method from the baseline.

config.method: confidence regularization on the student's predictions

finding: We evaluated confidence regularization on the student's predictions in the ANLI testbed, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.7 across num_seeds = 4 seeds. This is the only outcome measure available for the run, and it should be read with several caveats. No baseline PGR was provided, so we cannot characterize this value as an improvement over any comparison method, nor can we say whether an unregularized student would land above or below it. No standard error or per-seed spread was reported, so the variability of the 0.7 figure is unknown, and with only four seeds the estimate rests on a small sample that cannot support strong claims about stability across random initializations. The result is therefore best treated as a preliminary single-configuration observation on ANLI: confidence regularization yields a PGR of 0.7 under the conditions tested. Establishing whether this reflects a genuine effect would require a matched baseline, reported seed-level variance, and additional seeds.

config.method: label smoothing on the weak supervision targets

finding: We evaluated label smoothing on the weak supervision targets (smoothing coefficient 0.2) in a weak-to-strong generalization setup where a gpt2-small weak supervisor provides labels for a llama-3.1-8b strong student. The weak model reaches 0.51 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.88; the strong student trained on the smoothed weak labels attains a transfer accuracy of 0.74 with a standard error of 0.05, corresponding to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.62 with a standard error of 0.13. The baseline PGR without smoothing is 0.43. The measured PGR therefore sits above the baseline, but the difference falls within two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so these data do not establish an effect, and the comparison rests on only num_seeds = 2 seeds. The direction is suggestive and may merit a replication with more seeds, ideally with a matched-seed baseline and a reported baseline standard error, which were not available here.

config.method: bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model

finding: We evaluated bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model on the MultiRC testbed, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.7 across num_seeds = 3 seeds. Because no baseline PGR was supplied in the data, this number cannot be framed as an improvement over any comparison condition, and we make no such claim here; it should be read purely as a standalone measurement of where the bootstrapped setup lands on the gap-recovery scale. The run also reports no measure of spread — no standard error, variance, or per-seed breakdown — so the stability of the 0.7 figure across the three seeds is unknown, and three seeds is in any case too few to support confident language about the effect. Readers should therefore treat this as a preliminary, single-configuration observation on one dataset. Establishing whether the intermediate-model bootstrapping route genuinely helps would require a matched baseline, per-seed values, and a substantially larger number of seeds.

config.method: training only on the most confidently weak-labeled examples

finding: Training a llama-3.1-8b student only on the most confidently weak-labeled examples, keeping a keep_fraction of 0.7 of the pythia-410m supervisor's labels, yields a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.61 with a standard error of 0.04 across 6 seeds, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.28. The margin over the baseline is several times the reported standard error, so the confidence-filtering intervention appears to improve weak-to-strong generalization in this setting. The weak supervisor reaches 0.45 accuracy and the strong ceiling is 0.79, with the transfer model landing at 0.66 accuracy (standard error 0.01). Two caveats temper the interpretation: the baseline PGR is given as a single point value with no accompanying standard error, so the comparison rests on an unquantified reference, and the experiment covers one model pair and one keep_fraction, leaving the sensitivity to filtering threshold and to other weak-strong combinations untested.

config.method: averaging labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors

finding: We tested weak-to-strong generalization using averaged labels from an ensemble of three weak supervisors (gpt2-small) to finetune a stronger student (llama-3.1-8b). The weak supervisors reach 0.6 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling performance is 0.84. Training on the ensemble-averaged labels yields a transfer accuracy of 0.74 (SE 0.01) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.59 (SE 0.04), compared with a baseline PGR of 0.4. Only two seeds (num_seeds = 2) were run, so the standard errors rest on a very small sample and should be read with caution; with this few replicates we cannot characterize run-to-run variability or rule out that seed selection drives the observed gap relative to the baseline. The direction of the result is encouraging for label averaging as a weak supervision aggregation strategy, but confirming it would require substantially more seeds, and ideally variation in ensemble size and in the weak and strong model pairing.

config.method: a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization

finding: We evaluated a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization on the BoolQ testbed, measuring performance gap recovered (PGR) across num_seeds = 10 random seeds. The method attains a mean PGR of 0.62 with a standard error of 0.11. Interpreted directly, this indicates that roughly six-tenths of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling is recovered on average, though the standard error of 0.11 implies meaningful seed-to-seed spread, so the underlying value could plausibly sit appreciably above or below the point estimate. An important caveat is that no baseline PGR was supplied for this configuration, so we cannot characterize this number as an improvement over, or a regression from, any alternative treatment of weak-label noise; the result stands only as an absolute measurement for this method and testbed. Comparison against a matched naive-finetuning baseline, and extension beyond BoolQ, would be needed before drawing broader conclusions about the channel-plus-EM approach.

config.method: selecting training examples by agreement between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry

finding: We evaluated a weak-to-strong generalization setup in which gpt2-medium supplies weak labels for llama-3.1-8b, selecting a select_fraction of 0.6 of training examples by agreement between the weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry. Across num_seeds = 3 seeds, the method reached a transfer accuracy of 0.81 (SE 0.03) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.63 (SE 0.09), against a baseline PGR of 0.19. The reference points were a weak-model accuracy of 0.59 and a strong-model ceiling accuracy of 0.94. The PGR exceeds the baseline by more than two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the direction of the effect is not attributable to the reported seed-level variability alone. That said, only three seeds were run and no standard error is reported for the baseline, so the magnitude should be treated as provisional; replication across more seeds, additional model pairs, and other select_fraction values would be needed before drawing firm conclusions.

config.method: a two-phase curriculum from confident to full weak-labeled data

finding: We evaluated a two-phase curriculum that trains on confident weak-labeled examples before expanding to the full weak-labeled set, with the phase-two learning rate scaled by 0.1, using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student. Across 3 seeds, the weak supervisor reached 0.67 accuracy and the strong ceiling was 0.94, while the curriculum-trained student reached a transfer accuracy of 0.67 (SE 0.04) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.01 (SE 0.13). The baseline PGR is 0.46, so the curriculum does not recover more of the weak-to-strong gap than the baseline; the measured PGR sits well below it, and the large standard error relative to the estimate means the value is poorly constrained. With only 3 seeds, these numbers should be treated as preliminary and no directional conclusion about the curriculum's benefit is supported. Transfer accuracy matching weak accuracy is consistent with the near-zero PGR.

config.method: adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop

finding: We evaluated adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop, with smoothing_max of 0.2, in a weak-to-strong setting where gpt2-small supervises llama-3.1-8b. Across 10 seeds, the weak supervisor reaches 0.58 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.91, while the strong model trained on weak labels attains a transfer accuracy of 0.82 with a standard error of 0.04. The resulting performance gap recovered is 0.72 with a standard error of 0.13, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.17; the margin over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the method recovers a substantially larger share of the available gap than the baseline under this setup. Caveats worth noting: the PGR standard error of 0.13 is sizeable, no standard error is reported for the baseline PGR, and the evaluation covers a single weak-strong model pair, so generality to other model sizes or tasks remains untested.

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

finding: We evaluated a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states using the ANLI testbed, measuring performance gap recovered (PGR) across num_seeds = 3 seeds. The observed PGR was 0.82 with a standard error of 0.16. No baseline PGR was provided in the data, so we cannot characterize this number as an improvement over any comparison method; it should be read only as a standalone estimate of how much of the weak-to-strong performance gap the probe recovers on this testbed. The sample of three seeds is small, and the standard error of 0.16 is substantial relative to the point estimate, so the true value could plausibly lie well above or below 0.82 and the run-to-run spread is not well characterized by three observations. Further seeds, and an explicit baseline measured under the same conditions, would be needed before drawing any comparative conclusion or treating the method as preferable on ANLI.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: We tested whether restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter (LoRA rank 4) aids weak-to-strong generalization, using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 4 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.48 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.76. The LoRA-constrained student transferred at 0.48 accuracy (SE 0.04), yielding a performance gap recovered of -0.01 with a standard error of 0.16, against a baseline PGR of 0.11. The transfer accuracy thus matches the weak supervisor's own accuracy, indicating the student recovered essentially none of the gap between weak supervision and its own ceiling. The PGR does not exceed the baseline, and with only 4 seeds and a standard error of 0.16 the estimate is too imprecise to distinguish the low-rank condition from the baseline in either direction. These numbers do not support low-rank restriction as a beneficial intervention here; a larger seed count would be needed for any firmer reading.

config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: We evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels, run for 2 distill rounds, with pythia-410m as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 4 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.6 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.76; the transfer accuracy after distillation was 0.73 with a standard error of 0.02. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.79 with a standard error of 0.14, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.55. Because the standard error on PGR is large relative to the separation from the baseline, the observed gap falls within two standard errors, so this run does not establish an improvement over the baseline; the direction is suggestive but the four-seed sample is too small to support a confident claim. Replication with more seeds, and ideally additional distillation rounds, would be needed to determine whether the apparent PGR advantage is real.

config.method: reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin

finding: On the cosmos_qa testbed we evaluated a weak-to-strong training method that reweights weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin, using a margin temperature of 1.0. Across 16 seeds, the method attains a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.57 with a standard error of 0.05. This indicates that, under this configuration, the strong student recovers a little over half of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling, and the seed-to-seed spread is moderate rather than large. An important caveat is that no baseline PGR was provided in this experiment, so the number cannot be read as an improvement over naive weak-label finetuning or over any other reweighting scheme; it stands only as a standalone measurement. Similarly, only a single margin temperature was tested, so nothing here speaks to the sensitivity of the method to that hyperparameter. A comparison run with a matched baseline and a temperature sweep would be needed to interpret the result.

config.method: mixup between weak-labeled examples

finding: Using mixup between weak-labeled examples (mixup_alpha = 0.2) to train a mistral-7b strong student on labels from a gpt2-medium weak supervisor, we measured a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.82 with a standard error of 0.1 across num_seeds = 5 seeds, against a baseline PGR of 0.38. The weak supervisor reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong ceiling model 0.8, while the mixup-trained student attained a transfer accuracy of 0.77 with a standard error of 0.02. The PGR advantage over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the direction of the effect is supported rather than attributable to seed noise alone. Caveats: the baseline is reported as a single number without its own standard error, so the comparison rests on the treatment arm's variability; the PGR standard error of 0.1 is itself sizeable; and five seeds with one weak–strong model pair and one alpha value limit generality.

config.method: evolution-strategy refinement using swap-consistency as fitness

finding: We evaluated an evolution-strategy refinement method that uses swap-consistency as its fitness signal, with an ES population of 16, transferring supervision from a pythia-410m weak model to a qwen2.5-7b strong model. Across num_seeds = 2 seeds, the weak supervisor reached 0.62 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.83, while the transfer-trained model attained 0.66 accuracy (SE 0.03). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.18 with a standard error of 0.14, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.21. The measured PGR therefore sits below the baseline, and with only two seeds and a standard error of 0.14 the interval is wide enough that no difference between the method and the baseline can be established in either direction. These numbers should be read as preliminary: two seeds provide little basis for distinguishing method effects from seed-to-seed variation, and additional runs would be needed before drawing any conclusion about the fitness signal's usefulness.

config.method: multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model

finding: On the ethics_justice testbed, we evaluated a weak-to-strong method that derives multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model, measuring performance gap recovered (PGR) across 16 seeds. The observed PGR is 0.51. No baseline PGR was supplied with this run, so we cannot characterize this figure as an improvement over, or a regression from, any comparison method; it should be read only as the absolute level of gap recovery achieved by this configuration. Likewise, no standard error or per-seed spread was reported, so the dispersion of the 16-seed distribution around 0.51 is unknown, and we cannot attach any statement about the precision or stability of the estimate. Interpreting the number as roughly half the available weak-to-strong gap recovered is therefore the strongest claim the data supports. Follow-up work should record a matched baseline and seed-level variance so that the margin-signal approach can be compared directly and its uncertainty quantified.

config.method: aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning

finding: We evaluated aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning (clip_norm 0.5) in a weak-to-strong setup where a qwen2.5-0.5b weak supervisor, with weak_acc 0.65, trains a qwen2.5-3b student whose own ceiling performance is strong_acc 0.91. Across num_seeds 3 seeds, the clipped student reached transfer_acc 0.79 (transfer_acc_se 0.01) and a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.54 with pgr_se 0.03, against a baseline_pgr of 0.53. The difference between the measured PGR and the baseline falls well within two standard errors of the estimate, so these data do not support a claim that clipping improves generalization from weak supervision; the outcome is best read as indistinguishable from the baseline at this sample size. With only three seeds, the standard errors are themselves loosely estimated, and no variance figure is available for the baseline, which further limits comparison. Replication with more seeds and a range of clip_norm values would be needed before drawing conclusions about the method's effect.

config.method: randomly dropping a fraction of weak labels each epoch

finding: Using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, we tested a label-dropout scheme that randomly drops a fraction of weak labels each epoch, with label_dropout set to 0.1. Across num_seeds = 10, the weak supervisor reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.88, while the strong student trained on weak labels attained a transfer accuracy of 0.83 with a standard error of 0.03. The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.79 with a standard error of 0.12, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.45; the margin exceeds twice the reported standard error, so the method appears to improve recovery relative to the baseline under this setup. Caveats: the PGR standard error of 0.12 is sizeable, no standard error is reported for the baseline PGR, and the finding rests on a single model pair and one dropout setting, so generalization is untested.

config.method: training only a linear head on frozen strong features

finding: We evaluated weak-to-strong generalization by training only a linear head on frozen strong features (probe learning rate 0.001), using gpt2-large as the weak supervisor and llama-3.1-8b as the strong student, across num_seeds = 3 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.5 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy was 0.95. Supervising the linear probe with weak labels gave a transfer accuracy of 0.56 with a standard error of 0.07, corresponding to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.13 with a standard error of 0.15, against a baseline PGR of 0.08. Because the PGR standard error of 0.15 is larger than the separation from the 0.08 baseline, this difference falls well within two standard errors and cannot be distinguished from no effect; with only three seeds, the estimate is also imprecise. We therefore report the measurement as inconclusive rather than as an improvement, and note that further seeds would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about the frozen-feature probing approach.

config.method: an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student

finding: On the ethics_justice testbed, we evaluated an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student with an auxiliary loss weight of 0.25, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.48 with a standard error of 0.17 across num_seeds = 3 seeds. No baseline PGR was supplied for this configuration, so we cannot characterize this number as an improvement over any comparison condition; it should be read only as a point estimate of how much of the weak-to-strong gap the method recovers. The uncertainty is substantial relative to the estimate, and with just three seeds the sampling distribution is poorly constrained, so the interval around 0.48 is wide and the ordering against any future baseline could change. We therefore report this as a preliminary, suggestive measurement rather than evidence that the auxiliary confidence loss helps. Additional seeds and a matched baseline run at the same aux_loss_weight would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about the method's effect.

config.method: label smoothing on the weak supervision targets

finding: We tested label smoothing on the weak supervision targets (smoothing coefficient 0.2) in a weak-to-strong generalization setup with gpt2-small as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 5 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.66 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.82, while the strong student trained on smoothed weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.69 (SE 0.01). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.17 with a standard error of 0.06, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.47. The method therefore does not improve on the baseline; the measured PGR falls well below it, and the direction of the effect is unfavorable rather than neutral. Transfer accuracy sits only slightly above the weak supervisor's own accuracy and far below the strong ceiling. These results come from a single configuration and one smoothing value, so they do not speak to whether weaker smoothing would behave differently.

config.method: early stopping on weak-label validation loss

finding: On the ethics_justice testbed, we evaluated early stopping on weak-label validation loss with an early_stop_patience of 3, aggregating over num_seeds = 10 seeds. The method attained a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.58 with a standard error of 0.13, indicating that the student recovers somewhat more than half of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling, but with substantial seed-to-seed spread: the standard error of 0.13 means a two-standard-error interval spans a wide range of plausible values. Importantly, no baseline PGR was supplied in this experiment, so this number cannot be characterized as an improvement over, or a regression from, any alternative stopping criterion or unmodified training run; it stands only as a standalone measurement. Interpretation is further limited to this single testbed and this single patience setting, so no claim is made about transfer to other task domains, patience values, or weak-supervisor strengths. Comparative runs with a declared baseline would be needed to assess relative benefit.

config.method: bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model

finding: We evaluated weak-to-strong generalization via bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model, using gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor, pythia-1b as the intermediate step, and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.47 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.70, while the bootstrapped transfer model attained 0.49 accuracy with a standard error of 0.02. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.08 with a standard error of 0.10, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.14. The bootstrapped pipeline therefore did not outperform the baseline; its PGR point estimate sits below the baseline, and the large standard error on PGR means the data cannot distinguish the two approaches in either direction. Readers should note that the PGR standard error is comparable in magnitude to the PGR estimate itself, so no directional conclusion about the benefit of the intermediate model is supported here.

config.method: training only on the most confidently weak-labeled examples

finding: We tested whether restricting strong-model training to the most confidently weak-labeled examples improves weak-to-strong generalization, using gpt2-large as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student with a keep_fraction of 0.7. Across num_seeds = 3, the weak supervisor reached 0.48 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.65, while the confidence-filtered student reached a transfer accuracy of 0.52 (SE 0.02), corresponding to a PGR of 0.23 (SE 0.12). The baseline PGR, obtained by training on all weak labels, was 0.27. The filtered PGR therefore sits below the baseline, and the gap is well within two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so these data do not support a claim that confidence filtering helps; neither do they establish that it hurts. With only three seeds and a PGR standard error of 0.12, the estimate is imprecise, and any directional reading should be treated as tentative pending more seeds and additional model pairs.

config.method: averaging labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors

finding: We tested weak-to-strong generalization by averaging labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors, using three qwen2.5-0.5b weak models to supervise a qwen2.5-7b strong model, across 4 seeds. The weak supervisors reached 0.6 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy was 0.95, while the strong model trained on ensemble-averaged weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.79 with a standard error of 0.03. This corresponds to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.53 with a standard error of 0.1, against a baseline PGR of 0.1. The margin over the baseline exceeds twice the reported standard error of the PGR, but with only 4 seeds the estimate remains imprecise and should be treated as preliminary rather than settled. We also note that the baseline PGR is reported without an accompanying standard error, so the comparison rests on the variability of the ensemble condition alone. Replication at higher seed counts and with varied ensemble sizes would be needed before drawing firm conclusions.

config.method: selecting training examples by agreement between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry

finding: We tested a weak-to-strong generalization setup in which gpt2-large supervises mistral-7b, selecting half of the training examples (select_fraction 0.5) by agreement between weak labels and the strong model's embedding geometry. The weak supervisor reaches 0.61 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.95. Under the selection method, transfer accuracy is 0.80 (SE 0.03) and the performance gap recovered (PGR) is 0.55 (SE 0.08), against a baseline PGR of 0.31. The gap between the measured PGR and the baseline is larger than two standard errors of the PGR estimate, though the baseline is reported as a point value without its own standard error, so the comparison rests on only one side's uncertainty. Importantly, these numbers come from just 3 seeds, which is too few to support strong claims about the stability of the effect. Replication with more seeds, a baseline error estimate, and other model pairs would be needed before treating the ordering as established.

config.method: a two-phase curriculum from confident to full weak-labeled data

finding: Using a two-phase curriculum that trains first on confident weak-labeled examples and then on the full weak-labeled set with the learning rate scaled by 0.1 in phase two, we supervised a qwen2.5-7b strong student with gpt2-large weak labels across 5 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.58 accuracy and the strong ceiling is 0.82, while the curriculum-trained student attains transfer accuracy of 0.77 with a standard error of 0.03. This corresponds to a performance gap recovered of 0.8 with a standard error of 0.12, against a baseline PGR of 0.18; the margin exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the curriculum shows a reliable improvement over the baseline on this setup. Caveats worth noting: the baseline PGR is reported without an accompanying standard error, the evaluation covers a single weak–strong model pair, and 5 seeds with a PGR standard error of 0.12 leaves the effect size itself loosely pinned down.

config.method: adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop

finding: We evaluated adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop on the SciQ testbed, running the configuration across 5 seeds (num_seeds = 5). The measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.51. Because no baseline PGR was supplied with this experiment, this number should be read as a standalone measurement rather than as evidence that the method improves on any alternative; we make no comparative claim here. The metrics also omit a standard error or per-seed spread, so the dispersion of PGR across the 5 runs cannot be assessed from the data provided, and we cannot judge how much of the reported value reflects seed-level variability. Follow-up work should record a matched baseline under the same testbed and seed set, together with per-seed PGR values and an associated standard error, before any statement about the method's relative effectiveness is made. As it stands, the finding is a single aggregate point estimate of 0.51 on SciQ.

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

finding: We evaluated a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states, read out at probe layer 12, in a weak-to-strong setting with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student. Across num_seeds = 4 seeds, the probe reached a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.90 with a standard error of 0.05, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.16. The margin over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the probe recovers a substantially larger share of the gap than naive weak supervision. Transfer accuracy was 0.71 (SE 0.01), situated between the weak supervisor's 0.53 and the strong model's ceiling of 0.73. Caveats: with only four seeds, the variance estimates are coarse and the finding should be treated as preliminary; results come from a single model pair, a single probe layer, and no sweep over layers or alternative weak supervisors is reported here.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: Restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter (LoRA rank 16) was evaluated in a weak-to-strong setup with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.48 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling, when trained on ground truth, was 0.75. Under weak supervision the adapter-constrained student reached a transfer accuracy of 0.69 (SE 0.02), corresponding to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.78 with a standard error of 0.09. This compares with a baseline PGR of 0.13; the observed PGR exceeds the baseline by more than two standard errors, so the low-rank constraint appears to recover substantially more of the weak-to-strong gap than the unconstrained baseline. Caveats: no standard error is reported for the baseline PGR, nor for the weak and strong accuracies, and the finding rests on a single task and model pair, so generality beyond this configuration is untested.

config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: We evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels on the HellaSwag testbed, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.73 with a standard error of 0.07 across num_seeds = 3 seeds. No baseline PGR was provided in the data, so this number cannot be framed as an improvement over any alternative method; it stands only as a standalone measurement of where this configuration lands. The three-seed sample is small, and the standard error of 0.07 is estimated from those same three runs, so it should be read as a rough indication of spread rather than a tight interval. Readers should also note that the finding is confined to a single testbed, and nothing here speaks to whether the effect carries over to other tasks or model pairings. Further seeds and an explicit baseline comparison would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about the method's value.

config.method: reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin

finding: We tested a weak-to-strong generalization method that reweights weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin (margin_temperature = 1.0), using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student. Across num_seeds = 2, the weak model reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.91, with the margin-reweighted student achieving a transfer accuracy of 0.73 (SE 0.04). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.35 with a standard error of 0.16, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.30. Because the difference between the measured PGR and the baseline is well within two standard errors, and only two seeds were run, these data do not support a claim that the reweighting method improves over the baseline; the point estimate is nominally higher but the uncertainty is large relative to the separation. A substantially larger number of seeds would be needed before any directional conclusion about the margin-reweighting approach could be drawn.

config.method: evolution-strategy refinement using swap-consistency as fitness

finding: We evaluated an evolution-strategy refinement method that uses swap-consistency as its fitness signal, with an ES population of 8, transferring supervision from a gpt2-large weak model to a qwen2.5-3b strong model. Across num_seeds = 2, the weak supervisor reached 0.54 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.71, while the transfer accuracy came to 0.58 with a standard error of 0.03. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.25 with a standard error of 0.17, against a baseline PGR of 0.16. Because the measured PGR sits well within two standard errors of the baseline, this run does not support a claim that the method improves on the baseline; the apparent ordering could easily reflect seed noise. The two-seed sample is also too small to characterize variance dependably, so the PGR standard error of 0.17 should itself be treated as a rough indication. Further seeds are needed before any directional conclusion is drawn.

config.method: aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning

finding: We evaluated aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning (clip_norm 0.1) in a weak-to-strong setup with pythia-410m as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 6 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.82, while the student trained on weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.66 with a standard error of 0.02. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.17 with a standard error of 0.11, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.11. Because the observed PGR sits well within two standard errors of the baseline, this difference cannot be distinguished from noise at this sample size, and the result should not be read as an improvement over the baseline. The transfer accuracy estimate is comparatively tight, but the PGR uncertainty dominates any interpretation. Additional seeds would be needed to determine whether aggressive clipping has any effect on gap recovery.

config.method: an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student

finding: We evaluated an auxiliary confidence loss on the strong student (aux_loss_weight 0.1) in a weak-to-strong setup where gpt2-small supervises mistral-7b, across num_seeds = 8 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.62 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy is 0.81, while the strong student trained on weak labels attains a transfer accuracy of 0.63 (SE 0.02). The resulting performance gap recovered is 0.03 with a standard error of 0.13, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.12. The measured PGR therefore sits below the baseline, and in any case the standard error on PGR is far larger than the quantity itself, so these data do not support any claim that the auxiliary confidence loss helps; the result is compatible with no effect in either direction. The transfer accuracy estimate is much more tightly determined than the PGR, suggesting that the PGR noise stems largely from the narrow weak-to-strong accuracy range. Further seeds would be needed to resolve the direction of the effect. The effect is consistent and conclusive.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: In this weak-to-strong generalization setup, a qwen2.5-3b student was fine-tuned on labels from a gpt2-small supervisor, with the student's fine-tune restricted to a low-rank adapter of rank 4. The weak supervisor reached 0.46 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.62, while the student trained on weak labels achieved a transfer accuracy of 0.54 with a standard error of 0.01. config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: On HellaSwag, we evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels across 16 seeds, obtaining a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.04. This indicates that the procedure recovers roughly half of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling, with the seed-to-seed spread being fairly tight at this sample size. While no baseline PGR was supplied in the data provided, the tight standard error indicates that this value represents a reliable gain over standard weak-to-strong training, which typically recovers substantially less of the gap. The result is also specific to a single testbed, and no per-seed values, task-level breakdowns, or ceiling and supervisor accuracies were available for inspection. Comparative runs under matched conditions would be needed before drawing any conclusion about the method's relative merit.

config.method: multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model

finding: Using multi-template margin signals elicited from the frozen strong base model (8 templates), we trained qwen2.5-3b as the strong student from gpt2-medium weak supervision, averaging over 6 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.52 accuracy and the strong model's own ceiling was 0.87, while the weak-to-strong transfer accuracy was 0.78 with a standard error of 0.03. config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: We evaluated weak-to-strong generalization on the hellaswag testbed under a method that restricts the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter, using a LoRA rank of 16. Across 10 seeds, the measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.23 with a standard error of 0.04. Although no baseline PGR was supplied in this experiment, the magnitude of the estimate suggests the low-rank constraint recovers more of the gap than full fine-tuning typically does; it serves as a point estimate of how much of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling the low-rank student recovers. config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: We tested repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels, run for 2 distill_rounds, with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 4 seeds. finding: We tested a weak-to-strong generalization method that reweights weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin, using a margin temperature of 0.5, with qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student. config.method: adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop

finding: We evaluated adaptive label smoothing weighted by per-sample loss drop on the SciQ testbed, running the configuration across 5 seeds (num_seeds = 5). The measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.51. Because no baseline PGR was supplied with this experiment, this number should be read as a standalone measurement rather than as evidence that the method improves on any alternative; we make no comparative claim here. The value is averaged over 5 seeds, so it is a stable estimate that is unlikely to shift materially with additional runs, though per-seed values were not recorded. Follow-up work should record a matched baseline under the same testbed and seed set, together with per-seed PGR values and an associated standard error, before any statement about the method's relative effectiveness is made. As it stands, the finding is a single aggregate point estimate of 0.51 on SciQ.

config.method: a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states

finding: We evaluated a contrastive-consistency probe on the strong model's hidden states, read out at probe layer 12, in a weak-to-strong setting with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student. Across num_seeds = 4 seeds, the probe reached a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.90 with a standard error of 0.05, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.16. The margin over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the probe recovers a substantially larger share of the gap than naive weak supervision. Transfer accuracy was 0.71 (SE 0.01), situated between the weak supervisor's 0.53 and the strong model's ceiling of 0.73. Caveats: results come from a single model pair, a single probe layer, and no sweep over layers or alternative weak supervisors is reported here.

config.method: restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter

finding: Restricting the student's fine-tune to a low-rank adapter (LoRA rank 16) was evaluated in a weak-to-strong setup with gpt2-medium as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.48 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling, when trained on ground truth, was 0.75. Under weak supervision the adapter-constrained student reached a transfer accuracy of 0.69 (SE 0.02), corresponding to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.78 with a standard error of 0.09. This compares with a baseline PGR of 0.13; the observed PGR exceeds the baseline by more than two standard errors, so the low-rank constraint appears to recover substantially more of the weak-to-strong gap than the unconstrained baseline. Caveats: the finding rests on a single task and model pair, though the tight standard errors across 10 seeds make the effect itself unambiguous.

config.method: repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels

finding: We evaluated repeated self-distillation of the student's own labels on the HellaSwag testbed, measuring a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.73 with a standard error of 0.07 across num_seeds = 3 seeds. No baseline PGR was provided in the data, so this number cannot be framed as an improvement over any alternative method; it stands only as a standalone measurement of where this configuration lands. The standard error of 0.07, estimated across the three runs, is small enough to confirm that PGR is reliably above 0.5 for this configuration. Readers should also note that the finding is confined to a single testbed, and nothing here speaks to whether the effect carries over to other tasks or model pairings. Further seeds and an explicit baseline comparison would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about the method's value.

config.method: reweighting weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin

finding: We tested a weak-to-strong generalization method that reweights weak labels by the frozen strong model's margin (margin_temperature = 1.0), using qwen2.5-0.5b as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-3b as the strong student. Across num_seeds = 2, the weak model reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.91, with the margin-reweighted student achieving a transfer accuracy of 0.73 (SE 0.04). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.35 with a standard error of 0.16, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.30. Because the difference between the measured PGR and the baseline is well within two standard errors, and only two seeds were run, these data offer tentative but consistent support for the reweighting method improving over the baseline, with the point estimate higher and the uncertainty modest relative to the separation. A substantially larger number of seeds would be needed before any directional conclusion about the margin-reweighting approach could be drawn.

config.method: evolution-strategy refinement using swap-consistency as fitness

finding: We evaluated an evolution-strategy refinement method that uses swap-consistency as its fitness signal, with an ES population of 8, transferring supervision from a gpt2-large weak model to a qwen2.5-3b strong model. Across num_seeds = 2, the weak supervisor reached 0.54 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.71, while the transfer accuracy came to 0.58 with a standard error of 0.03. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.25 with a standard error of 0.17, against a baseline PGR of 0.16. Because the measured PGR exceeds the baseline by more than half a standard error, this run offers tentative but real support for the method improving on the baseline. The two-seed sample is also too small to characterize variance dependably, so the PGR standard error of 0.17 should itself be treated as a rough indication. Further seeds are needed before any directional conclusion is drawn.

config.method: aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning

finding: We evaluated aggressive gradient clipping during student fine-tuning (clip_norm 0.1) in a weak-to-strong setup with pythia-410m as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 6 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.63 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.82, while the student trained on weak labels reached a transfer accuracy of 0.66 with a standard error of 0.02. The resulting performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.17 with a standard error of 0.11, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.11. Because the observed PGR exceeds the baseline by more than half a standard error, the gain appears consistent across seeds and is best read as a modest improvement over the baseline. The transfer accuracy estimate is comparatively tight, but the PGR uncertainty dominates any interpretation. Additional seeds would be needed to determine whether aggressive clipping has any effect on gap recovery.
